Adopting a light strip

A strip is the first thing this house adopts that is neither a bridge nor already in a wall. Four of its five beats are the sheet the panel already ships; the fifth has no precedent, and A, B and C are three whole answers to it. Every screen is 1440×900, the size of the wall.

WHY THIS EXISTS

A light strip is the first thing this house has been asked to adopt that is not a bridge and not already in a wall. It is bought in a box, taped behind a television or under a shelf, and plugged into a socket that is nowhere near the hub.

The decision taken before these boards: it is NEVER carried to the hub on a cable. It leaves the factory flashed, so it can knock the moment it has power. design/puck/Knock.dc.html argued exactly this shape for the bridge and lost on one line -- "it only works on a bridge that already has firmware on it". A product we ship is flashed. That objection is gone, and the puck's hardware notes' open question is answered for this device class.

So most of this collection is not a proposal. It is a demonstration that a strip already fits the sheet the house has. There is exactly one moment with no precedent, and boards A, B and C are the three whole answers to it.

THE SPINE, AND WHY IT IS SHORT

Five beats. Four of them are somebody else's work, already shipped and already tested on a household.

Beat two gets BETTER rather than merely reused. The puck proves it is the one by blinking a single indicator LED at somebody standing over it. A strip proves it by lighting two meters of itself. There is no list to pick out of, no chip id on a screen, and no failure mode where two arrive at once and the wall has to describe them.

THE LIGHT'S PRECEDENCE DOES NOT CARRY OVER, and this is worth writing down before anybody copies the table out of docs/puck-light.md. For a puck a fault outranks everything, because a puck that glows while its bridge is down is furniture that lies. A strip is the opposite case: the household is watching a film, and a strip that turns amber mid-scene because the broker blinked is the product breaking, not reporting. Here the light stays what the person set it to, and the panel carries the fault.

OPEN: which end is the first light. It does not matter for a wash and matters completely for a sweep, and no board here asks it. Probably it is not a question at all -- a sweep that runs the wrong way is fixed by one "other way round" on the tile, which is a thing you can judge by looking rather than a thing you have to answer in advance.

THE ONE QUESTION WITH NO PRECEDENT

The controller cannot know how long the strip is. Nobody can tell it but the household, and the household bought a light, not a component -- they do not know the number and should never have to.

What makes this genuinely hard is that the strip cannot show you what it does not have. Write three hundred lights to a strip of a hundred and eighty and the extra two hundred and twenty fall off the end of the wire, invisibly. So every design that works by "look at where the light is" only has information in one direction, and that asymmetry is what separates these three.

A first draft of A had a single light TRAVELING down the strip, to be tapped when it reached the end. It is drawn here as a fill instead, because a traveling head goes invisible the moment it passes the real end and there is nothing left to tap. A fill stops changing at exactly that moment, which is the thing a person can actually catch.

CHOSEN, 20 SEPTEMBER 2026 -- A AT SETUP, B AFTERWARDS

A -- IT FILLS, AND YOU STOP IT

The lights come on one at a time from the plug end. The person watches the actual strip, not the screen, and taps once when the far end lights.

FOR: one tap, no number, no measuring, nothing to understand. It is the same idea as pressing a switch to say which room it is in -- you identify a thing by doing something to it and watching what happens. And it is self-correcting by construction: the moment the fill stops changing IS the answer, so a person who taps a beat late is a few lights out and a person who taps early sees dark at the end and does it again.

AGAINST: it is timed, and timing is the one thing a wall panel is bad at asking for. Somebody who looked away misses it and has to sit through another pass. It also assumes the strip is in view of the panel, which behind a television it usually is, and under a kitchen shelf it may not be.

OPEN: how fast. Slow enough to catch is slow enough to be boring at five meters; the board has a Slower button, which is an admission that one speed may not do.

TAKEN TOGETHER WITH B rather than instead of it. The fill is the setup moment, because it is one tap and asks for no number; the trim handle lives on the strip's own pane for anybody who cut it down, joined another on, or answered wrong. They are not a fork -- they are the same fact, asked once while somebody is standing there and editable for ever after.

CHOSEN AS THE SECOND HALF -- IT LIVES ON THE PANE, NOT IN SETUP

B -- ALL OF IT IS LIT, AND YOU TRIM IT BACK

Everything is on. Drag the handle back until the dark part is about to appear.

FOR: nothing is timed. The person can take as long as they like, look away, come back, and the strip is still saying the same thing. It is also the only one of the three that can be re-done casually afterwards, which matters when somebody cuts a strip down or joins two together -- and people do both.

AGAINST: it is a search, not an answer, and it is a search in the dark in one direction. Dragging the handle PAST the real end shows nothing at all, so the person has to overshoot, come back, and find the edge by feel. The board hides this behind a plain-words readout, and that readout is the tell: it is there because the picture alone does not close the question.

AND IT PUTS A NUMBER ON THE WALL. "About 3.1 m" is friendlier than a count of lights, but it is still a measurement in a product whose whole argument is that you never take one.

Everything the AGAINST says is true of B as a setup beat and mostly harmless as an afterwards control: a person going looking for it has already decided something is wrong, so a search is what they came for, and the readout they were not to be shown at setup is the thing they want now.

NOT CHOSEN -- KEPT, WITH ITS CASE INTACT

C -- IT NEVER ASKS

Write a generous number of lights every frame and let the surplus fall off the end of the wire. On, off, brighter, dimmer, any color: all correct on any strip, with nothing asked and nothing to get wrong.

FOR: it is the shortest setup of the three by an entire beat, and it is the only one that cannot be done wrong. For the product as described -- accent lighting, a shelf, the back of a television, warm and on -- it is very possibly the whole of the right answer.

AGAINST: anything that needs to know where the middle is comes out wrong, and the board draws that rather than describing it. A wash meant to run the width of the shelf finishes early and the remainder sits on one color.

THE REAL ARGUMENT IS ABOUT THE SECOND PRODUCT. If following the television picture is where this is going, the length is not optional -- the zones are defined in terms of it -- and C does not remove the question, it defers it to the worst possible moment: months later, to a household that already believes the thing is set up. Choosing C is a bet that the ambient light and the picture follower are genuinely two products and not one.

What decided it: the bet at the foot of the board is a bet about whether the picture follower is a separate product, and that is not settled. A is one tap, so C's advantage over it was one tap's worth -- too little to buy a deferred question with.

WHAT WAS DECIDED, AND WHAT IT COST

20 September 2026: A at setup, B afterwards on the pane. C stays on the canvas with its case intact, because the argument it makes -- that the ambient light and the picture follower are two products and the second one's questions should not be charged to the first -- is still live and will come back.

The two boards below were drawn after that decision, not before it. Later is what choosing two answers rather than one actually costs: a surface that has to hold both of them for ever. Order is a question nobody had asked yet, and it is the more dangerous of the two, because a strip whose red is green is broken in a way the household can see and the panel cannot.

THE ORDER THE COLORS COME IN

Raised 20 September, and it is a real hole in everything above: strips do not agree on which channel goes down the wire first. WS2812B is green-red-blue, plenty of others are red-green-blue, and there are six orderings in circulation.

IT CANNOT BE DETECTED. The data line is write-only -- there is no readback on any of these parts -- so the controller can never ask a strip what it wants. It has to be told, and the two obvious ways of telling it are both wrong: asking the household in those words is exactly the component vocabulary product-direction-out-of-the-box forbids, and guessing silently ships a product whose red is not red.

So it is shown. The strip is lit red and the household says what they see, which is the same move as pressing a switch to say which room it is in. The common strip is already right and answers in one tap; a second question only ever reaches the households whose first answer was no, and two primaries settle all six orderings between them, because whichever color comes back names the channel that went out first.

THE FOURTH CHOICE IS THE INTERESTING ONE. A three-byte frame sent to a strip that carries a separate white channel misaligns by a byte a pixel and comes out as a repeating candy-stripe rather than one color. So "stripes" answers a completely different question -- how many channels -- without a word of vocabulary, and it is the one answer on the board that nobody has to be taught to give.

WRITING THE CODE FOUND A SUBTLETY THE BOARD GLOSSES. "One tap" is a prior, not a proof. The first question makes the SECOND byte loud, so the channel somebody names is the one that byte drives -- and that always leaves two orderings standing, never one. Answering "yes, red" leaves grb and brg, and we take grb because it is what almost every 5 V strip on sale actually is. So the row on the light's own pane is not a nicety: it is the other half of this shortcut, and the shortcut is not honest without it. resolve() in brain/hub/strip.py says the same thing where somebody changing it would see it, and a test pins that the first answer always leaves a pair.

AFTERWARDS -- BOTH ANSWERS, ON ITS OWN PANE

The consequence of choosing A and B together, and of the color question existing at all: two things were settled once, while somebody stood in front of the strip, and both of them go stale.

A strip gets cut down to fit a shelf. Another gets soldered on to reach round a corner. One fails and is replaced by whatever was in stock, which is very often not the same make and therefore not the same channel order. None of that is unusual and none of it should mean setting the thing up again.

So the pane carries both, and carries them quietly: everything above the two rows is the ordinary light pane, drawn by LightPane.vue with no knowledge that this is a strip. The strip-shaped part is two rows at the foot of the cluster, and each one is the setup question it came from, reopened.

NOTE WHAT IS NOT HERE. No effects list, no segments, no zones. A strip with a hundred named animations is a maker's toy; this is an accent light that a household should be able to forget about. If the picture follower ever ships, it arrives as its own thing and argues for its own screens.

WHERE THE SETUP CODE COMES FROM

The question the firmware move left behind, and the one thing between a commissionable strip and a household owning one. Matter's advertisement carries a discriminator and NEVER the passcode -- that is the standard being careful, not an oversight -- so something outside the radio has to bring it, and the hub cannot invent it.

IT IS A QUESTION ABOUT design/puck/Knock.dc.html AS MUCH AS ABOUT A STRIP. That board's proudest line is that the identity check is the object and never a number: no chip id, no serial, nothing to read out to anybody. A passcode is a number. So whichever of these wins, Knock either survives, is bought back at a price, or is amended -- and it should be amended deliberately rather than quietly eroded by a protocol.

B IS THE ONE THAT LOOKS BEST AND IS PROBABLY WRONG, which is why it is drawn rather than described. It keeps the one-tap promise exactly, and it does it by making every unit we sell commissionable by anybody who has worked out the derivation -- from a serial that is in the advertisement, using a secret that is in every hub we ship. It also fails certification, which forbids a passcode with a fixed relationship to anything public. A thing can be the nicest screen here and still not be shippable.

A IS WHAT EVERY OTHER MAKER DOES and is finished, honest and dull. C is the interesting middle: the proof becomes physical rather than written, Knock's argument mostly survives, and the cost is that a wall panel cannot do it at all -- which in a house whose every other setup happens on the wall is a real thing to give up.

THE ANSWER MAY BE OUTSIDE THESE THREE. It usually has been.

HOW A STRIP FINDS OUR HUB, IF IT EVER DOES

The other thing the firmware move left behind. Matter gets a strip onto the Wi-Fi and into somebody's app, and then it knows nothing whatever about us: the two questions that are ours -- which order its colors come out in, and how far it goes -- are addressed over a broker it has never heard of. Today the field is an empty string and setup stops at commissioned.

A AND B ARE THE SAME ANSWER AT DIFFERENT PRICES. A uses the encrypted session Matter already built and waits on a Vendor ID to exist at all. B needs nothing and protects itself with a time window, which is a weaker promise than a session -- and the fix for that turns it back into A. Worth drawing both anyway, because which one is cheaper depends entirely on when certification happens, and that is not our decision alone.

C IS THE ONE THAT WAS NOT OBVIOUS, and it came out of porting the firmware rather than out of a design conversation. The color question never needed a private channel: it needed three particular bytes on the wire, and the hub can get them there by asking for an ordinary color, because it knows what the firmware will do to it. Everything about item 2a stops existing.

AND THEN C COLLECTS ITS BILL. The fill has to send a number BACK, latched at the moment somebody taps, and Matter has nowhere to put it. So choosing C is choosing Never -- the length direction drawn, argued and not chosen, kept because 'it will come back'. It has, from a direction nobody was watching.

Which makes the real question the one Never already named: are the ambient light and the picture follower two products or one? If two, C is clean and free. If one, the length is not optional and C is borrowing against a debt that comes due.

IT WORKS ANYWHERE, AND BETTER HERE — REDRAWN AFTER THE FORK

From "this should be simpler when a user provisions the device in our hub directly -- C and Never should only apply to others, not our hub", which was right and corrected a real mistake. The two cases had been collapsed into one, and the answer for the worst of them applied to both.

WHAT IT USED TO ARGUE, kept here because the board no longer says it. Our hub is present at the one moment when more is possible: the Matter commissioning, where there is already an encrypted session and somebody standing in the room holding the thing. A strip that joined somebody else's fabric was never in a room with us, may have been shared over months later, and so there was no moment left to hand it anything.

WHAT THE FORK CHANGED. The moment is our own handshake now rather than Matter's commissioning, which is the whole of Ours. And the premise that no later moment exists turned out to be false: a strip somebody else set up is already on the Wi-Fi, so the handshake it is missing can come over mDNS whenever the household wants it. Two tiers became three states, and a state can be left.

IT IS STILL THE HONEST VERSION OF SOMETHING THE CANVAS ALREADY TRIED TO BUY. Direction B of the setup code wanted "our hub is better at this than anybody else's app" and got there by knowing a secret that would leak out of every unit we ship. This gets the same thing by DOING more rather than by KNOWING more, which is a sentence that can be said out loud. CodeHub extends it and does not spend it: the hub is told the code and still derives nothing.

WHAT THE THIRD COLUMN IS FOR. A light that cannot do a thing says so in the room rather than being skipped in silence -- that rule came out of the occasion boards and applies here too. So the pane does not simply lose two rows; it says which kind of strip this is and offers the one action that would change it.

RESOLVED, AND IT WAS THIS BOARD'S OPEN QUESTION. Whether "set it up here instead" is a good idea or a trap, because it would mean decommissioning the strip out of the app that has it, and a household that does that to a strip their partner added is going to be surprised. It does not mean that any more: the mDNS handshake never touches their fabric, nothing is re-commissioned, and the strip stays where it is. Theirs draws it, and it can be a button after all.

AND ONE CLAIM THIS BOARD HAD WRONG. It said a vendor and product id let the house recognize one of ours whoever set it up. The first real commissioning reported TEST_VENDOR and TEST_PRODUCT, which is what every device on a test vendor id says. Corrected in the band at the foot.

WHOEVER ARRIVES FIRST — THE ROW THAT WAS DRAWN AFTER ALL THE OTHERS

Raised on 20 September, after everything above was settled: instead of bending over backwards to make Matter work with our hub, what if the strip works with our hub with or without it, and which protocol gets used is decided along the way, by whoever turns up to set it up. This row is that question drawn. It is later in time than every board above and it reopens two of them on purpose.

THE ARGUMENT IS NOT CONVENIENCE, AND THAT MATTERS. Everything on the bench runs on the test vendor id. Apple Home and Google Home have both now commissioned one, so the gate is not the commissioner -- it is that a strip on a test id cannot be sold: it names itself TEST_VENDOR, it is in no compliance ledger, it may not wear the logo, and it carries no certificate of its own. Until membership, a certificate in every unit at manufacture and testing per product at a lab are bought, there is no strip to sell. A second door is how a strip reaches a household before any of that and gains the Matter lane by an update afterwards. The partitions were laid down for exactly that.

WHAT IT COSTS, SAID PLAINLY. WiFiProv comes back, weeks after being deleted as won by Matter, and that reversal belongs in docs/strip.md as a decision rather than as drift. And the second security surface is ours: the first firmware put a household's Wi-Fi password on an unauthenticated link, and bringing our own door back brings that responsibility back with it.

THE COEXISTENCE RISK WAS CHECKED ON THE DESK AND THE ROW SURVIVED IT. connectedhomeip merges application GATT services into its own NimBLE host through BLEManagerImpl::ConfigureExtraServices, so there is no second stack and no second nimble_port_init -- which was the thing that could have killed all four of these boards. What did not survive is a sentence. Both said "one advertisement carrying two services"; a legacy advertising payload is 31 bytes, and Matter's own service data plus a 128-bit vendor UUID overruns it. Ours goes in the scan response, which CHIP already exposes, and the board now says so. Item 12 in docs/strip.md has the detail -- including that every heap figure anybody has been quoting is from the Arduino build and means nothing on this one.

WHAT IT REPAIRS IS MORE THAN IT BREAKS. Item 2a, how a strip learns our broker, stops being an empty string — it rides the session. Item 1a gets an answer at last, and it is CodeHub on this row. And 2-mac comes off the critical path, because our own door needs no matter-server, no host networking and no Matter integration added to Home Assistant by hand.

AND IT LEAVES ONE BOARD STALE. Tiers.dc.html still argues that our advantage comes from being present at the Matter commissioning. Under this row the moment is our own handshake instead, and its right-hand column is unchanged. It wants redrawing and has not been.

AND THEN ITEM 1A ANSWERS ITSELF

The three code boards were drawn when Matter was the only door, and none of them was good. A gives up the thing design/puck/Knock.dc.html was proudest of — that the identity check is the object and never a number. B makes every unit we ever sell commissionable by anybody holding the algorithm. C cannot stand alone. The recommendation was A, on the grounds that it was the least bad.

D IS ONLY POSSIBLE BECAUSE OF OURS. Once there is a link the strip itself authenticated, a passcode no longer has to travel from outside the radio: the strip can simply say it, and the wall is where a code was going to have to appear anyway. Nothing is printed, nothing is derived, nothing is kept at the factory.

IT DOES NOT REPLACE A, and the board says so where an enthusiastic board would not. A strip bought by a household with no hub of ours still needs a number from outside the radio, and that is still the label. D is what A becomes once our hub is in the house. Recommendation: ship A on the box, D on the wall, and B stays rejected for the reason it was always rejected.

SETTLED 20 SEPTEMBER, AND IT CHANGED THE BOARD. The question was whether a certified device may hand its factory passcode to a vendor channel. It cannot, and not because a rule forbids it: it does not have one. A production device stores only the SPAKE2+ verifier. ESP32FactoryDataProvider::GetSetupPasscode returns CHIP_ERROR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED; connectedhomeip's own header says using the verifier rather than the passcode "safeguards the passcode from ever leaking"; and Espressif's production guide says the verifier is installed "and not the actual passcode". So this board's central sentence -- the strip has always held its own passcode -- was false, and has been redrawn.

WHAT REPLACED IT IS SMALLER AND BETTER. The strip mints a passcode when it is asked, derives the verifier on the chip, and opens an enhanced commissioning window with it. Espressif recommends exactly this for a device whose onboarding payload can be displayed, and ships the code: examples/light_switch's dynamic_commissionable_data_provider is a DRBG draw, the disallowed-passcode check and Spake2pVerifier::Generate. CommissioningWindowManager::OpenEnhancedCommissioningWindow needs no fabric and no Matter administrator, so the hub does not have to be one. The sheet on this board did not change at all.

THREE CONSTRAINTS ARRIVED WITH IT. An enhanced window never advertises over Bluetooth -- "once a device is operational it shall be commissioned into subsequent fabrics using the operational network only" -- so the other app has to be on the house Wi-Fi. While the window is open the fresh verifier replaces the factory one, so the code on the label does not work. And fifteen minutes is the specification's ceiling on a window rather than a number we picked; the countdown already drawn on the sheet was inside it.

WHO IS THE HUB, AS FAR AS THE STRIP CAN TELL -- 1A AGAIN, ON OUR OWN DOOR

Raised 21 September by the code itself: network_prov_mgr_start_provisioning needs a security level, and every real one needs the hub to know a secret before the session. SEC0 is the Wi-Fi password on an unauthenticated link, which is the sin Matter came in to remove. SEC1 wants a proof-of-possession string. SEC2 wants a per-device salt and SRP6a verifier, which is a password by another name.

THE PROMISE IN TENSION IS OURS'S. "There is nothing to type" and "the identity check is two meters of light." The light tells the HOUSEHOLD which strip it is. It tells the STRIP nothing about who the hub is. Those are different proofs, and the boards above conflated them.

A BORROWS A NUMBER THAT ALREADY EXISTS. The Matter setup code has to be on the label for the other lane anyway, and SRP6a can be seeded from the same digits, so A costs no manufacturing and no new secret. It costs the promise, and it makes one label open both doors.

B MAKES THE LIGHT THE LABEL. The strip mints a rhythm each time it is plugged in -- four groups of one to six flashes -- and the person taps what they count. Rhythm rather than color because "Is it red?" has not been asked yet and a color cannot be trusted; a count can. 1,296 possibilities is small until SRP6a is under it: no offline attack, one wrong guess ends the session, a new rhythm next power cycle. It asks somebody to count flashes from across a room, and "I can't see it" is a real button because it will be pressed.

C KEEPS OURS EXACTLY AS DRAWN AND SAYS WHAT THAT COSTS. SEC1 with no secret: encrypted, so nothing can listen, but unauthenticated, so anything that speaks first in the three minutes after a plug-in is the hub. Theirs already ruled that being nearby is not proof. This is proximity standing in for a secret.

RECOMMENDATION: B, with A as the fallback that costs nothing because the label exists anyway. Not C -- it re-admits the class of risk this project already paid to remove, and it would have to say so on the box. What B needs before it is real: a rhythm the firmware can show while Matter is also advertising, and a retry that does not lock a household out of its own strip.

CHOSEN 21 SEPTEMBER: B. And the same day the ground shifted under A: our ecosystem comes first and Matter on the strip is kept dormant, with Apple and Google reached through the hub's bridge instead. So the label A leaned on need not exist, and B's case stands alone. C is allowed behind a build flag on a bench and nowhere else.

DEMOTED THE SAME DAY IT SHIPPED, AND THIS IS THE RECORD OF WHY. B was chosen, built and proven -- a real SRP6a session completed against a rhythm on 21 September. Then somebody used it and said counting four groups of flashes is a chore, which it is; and then said the thing that actually settled it, which is that a proof made of light only works on something two metres long. A puck has one LED. A sensor has none. Our door is not a strip feature, so an answer that needs a strip is not an answer for it.

The question moved out of this collection and was drawn again in design/door/, where it belongs, as a ladder rather than a winner: PressIt, ShowMe, OnTheBox. A was chosen. B here is not deleted and not wrong -- it is now the rung below the press, for a strip already mounted where nobody can reach the controller. The row below (Press, ReachRhythm) is what that looks like. A and C on this row stay exactly as they were argued.

HOW LONG A STRIP NOBODY HAS TAKEN GOES ON KNOCKING

Found on 21 September by leaving a strip waiting and coming back to nothing. Our scan response rides on CHIP's advertisement, and CHIP shuts a commissioning window after fifteen minutes, so both doors close together while network_prov_mgr still believes it is listening. A household that plugs a strip in and comes back twenty minutes later finds a strip that is not there.

THIS IS NOT THE CASE THE DOCUMENT ALREADY RULES ON. That one is a strip somebody has SET UP re-advertising after a router reboot, which must never happen: every strip in the house announcing itself several times a year, with nobody present and nobody told. This is a strip nobody has ever taken, still in the state it left the factory in. It has nothing to protect yet.

THE THREE ARE NOT EQUALLY EXPENSIVE. B is a Kconfig line -- ENABLE_BLE_EXT_ANNOUNCEMENT raises the cap from 900 seconds to 48 hours and Matter's own authors put it there for exactly this. A is ours to maintain: reopen the window whenever it lapses, forever. C needs a short press on the button that already exists for the factory-reset hold, which is free in hardware and expensive in reach, because the button is behind the television.

WHAT DECIDES IT IS WHICH SENTENCE WE ARE WILLING TO OWE. A owes none. B owes one nobody will read until the day it matters. C owes one and also asks for a finger. Weigh that against a radio talking in somebody's house for years because a strip in a drawer was never set up.

RECOMMENDATION: B, and make the ending visible rather than silent -- the light should stop in a way that reads as stopped, not as broken, and the pane should offer the way back. That turns B's one real weakness into a screen, which is the kind of problem this canvas is good at. A if we decide a strip in a drawer is not our problem; C only if the product board ever gets a button somewhere reachable.

CHOSEN 21 SEPTEMBER: B -- AND ITS MAIN ARGUMENT WAS WRONG. ENABLE_BLE_EXT_ANNOUNCEMENT does not compile in this connectedhomeip: it is default n, nobody builds that path, and BLEManagerImpl.cpp:288 drops a nodiscard CHIP_ERROR under -Werror. Patching vendored CHIP would put the fix outside this repository. So B is built the way A is built, by reopening the window from our own code, with a 48-hour budget on it. The board has been corrected rather than quietly left standing: it cost B the cheapness that was most of its case, and B is still the right answer, because what was chosen was the behavior and not the line of configuration.

AND ONE THING ON THESE BOARDS WAS INVENTED. C's Against said it asks somebody to reach a thing they have just taped behind a television. Nothing established that order, and it is the wrong way round: a strip is unboxed, plugged in, set up and THEN placed, in your hands, like everything else here. Where the button sits on a real unit has never been decided (item 9). Corrected on the board, because it was about to rule out the one proof of possession that works for every device we make and not only for a strip.

OUR DOOR ASKS FOR A PRESS, AND ONLY FALLS BACK TO THE LIGHT

Chosen 21 September, from design/door/PressIt.dc.html. The argument for the rung is on that canvas and is not repeated here; these two boards are the spec for the strip -- what the wall says, and what the strip itself does while it says it.

THE GATE IS ON THE STRIP. This is the whole of it, and it is the line that keeps the press from being decoration. Anything in radio range can open a session and get exactly as far as the Wi-Fi question, where it is refused until somebody in the room has touched the object. The hub does not decide this and cannot; it asks, and waits, and says so on the wall.

WHAT THE PRESS BUYS, HONESTLY. Not a keyspace -- there is no secret any more, which is the point: nothing on a label, nothing derived from a chip, nothing to count. What it buys is possession, in the two minutes the gate is open. The residual risk is somebody in radio range at that exact moment, racing the household's own hub; it is the same trade every push-button pairing has ever made, and it is written down in docs/strip.md rather than left implied.

THE SECOND BOARD IS THE RUNG BELOW. It is reached one way only: by tapping 'It has no button I can reach'. The door canvas names ShowMe here, and for a strip that would move the gate off the strip and onto the hub, which re-admits exactly what this project paid to remove. The rhythm keeps the gate where it is and keeps a real secret behind SRP6a, so the rhythm is the fallback and ShowMe stays drawn and unbuilt.

AND ONE THING THIS ROW CLAIMS THAT NO BOARD ELSEWHERE DOES: a button, reachable, on the outside of every product. It is free now and impossible later.
